questions.question: In an extensive-form game, what does a system of beliefs $\mu$ assign?
options: To each information set, a probability distribution over the nodes in it
To each information set, a probability distribution over the actions available there
A single probability distribution over all the terminal nodes of the game tree
To each player, a probability distribution over the strategies of the opponents

questions.question: In an extensive-form game, what is meant by an assessment?
options: A system of beliefs $\mu$ together with the prior probabilities of Nature
A strategy profile $\sigma$ together with a system of beliefs $\mu$
A strategy profile $\sigma$ together with the payoffs it yields
A collection of information sets together with the actions at each

questions.question: For a node $x$ in an information set $h$ of an extensive-form game, what does the belief $\mu(x)$ measure?
options: The probability that play reaches node $x$, measured from the root
The probability that the player chooses a given action at node $x$
The mover's probability of being at $x$, given that $h$ has been reached
The probability that the information set $h$ is reached during play

questions.question: An information set $h=\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}$ has three nodes. Which triple $\big(\mu(x_1),\mu(x_2),\mu(x_3)\big)$ is a valid belief on $h$?
Player 2 has three information sets: one with $2$ nodes, one with $3$ nodes and one singleton. How many numbers must be chosen freely to specify her part of a system of beliefs?

Nature makes an entrant competitive or weak, each with probability $\frac{1}{2}$; the incumbent sees entry but not the type. Under $\sigma$, the competitive type always enters and the weak type enters with probability $\frac{1}{3}$. Which belief $\mu=\mathbb{P}(\text{competitive}\mid\text{entry})$ is consistent with $\sigma$?
In an extensive-form game of perfect information, every information set is a singleton. What does any system of beliefs look like?
options: It sets $\mu(x)$ equal to the probability that play reaches $x$ under $\sigma$
It may put any value $\mu(x)\in[0,1]$ on the single node $x$
It puts $\mu(x)=\frac{1}{2}$ on each node, as nothing is known about play
It puts $\mu(x)=1$ on the single node $x$ of every information set

questions.question: An entrant is of type $A$, $B$ or $C$ with prior probabilities $0.5$, $0.3$, $0.2$. Type $A$ always enters, $B$ enters with probability $0.5$, $C$ never enters. What belief over $(A,B,C)$ after entry is consistent with this behaviour?
options: $\left(\frac{2}{3},\ \frac{1}{3},\ 0\right)$

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $L$, $M$, $R$ or Out with probabilities $0.2$, $0.3$, $0$ and $0.5$. Out ends the game; after $L$, $M$ or $R$, player 2 moves at one information set $\{x_L,x_M,x_R\}$. Which beliefs $\big(\mu(x_L),\mu(x_M),\mu(x_R)\big)$ agree with these probabilities?
options: $\left(\frac{1}{3},\ \frac{1}{3},\ \frac{1}{3}\right)$

questions.question: What role do beliefs play when evaluating actions at an information set with several nodes?
options: The belief tells the player which node of the set has actually been reached
The player may choose different actions at the different nodes of the set
Payoffs in an extensive-form game are random even when all moves are known
Beliefs weight the continuation payoffs at the different nodes, which may differ.

questions.question: Assume perfect recall. At an information set with two or more nodes, what are the mover's beliefs about?
options: Earlier moves she did not observe, such as Nature's type draw or a rival's action
Later actions of her opponents, which their strategies have not yet revealed to her
Her own earlier actions, which she may have forgotten by the time she moves again
The payoffs at the terminal nodes, which she learns only once the game has ended

questions.question: Which statement about the relation between the payoffs of an extensive-form game and a system of beliefs is correct?
options: $\mu$ is found by best-responding to the payoffs at each information set
$\mu$ puts all weight on the node where the mover's payoff is highest
Payoffs alone do not determine $\mu$; it is specified together with $\sigma$
$\mu$ has no effect on which action is optimal, only on payoffs

questions.question: In a finite extensive-form game with perfect recall, under a strategy profile $\sigma$, information set $h$ is reached with positive probability. How many belief distributions on $h$ agree with the conditional probabilities of its nodes given $h$?
options: Exactly one, $\mu(x)=\mathbb{P}_\sigma(x)/\mathbb{P}_\sigma(h)$ for each $x\in h$
Every distribution on $h$, since beliefs are chosen along with $\sigma$
Two: one placing all weight on a single node, the other spreading it
None, unless every player uses a pure strategy under $\sigma$

questions.question: Under a strategy profile $\sigma$, information set $h$ is reached with probability $0$. Why does Bayes' conditioning formula not determine beliefs at $h$?
options: Every node of $h$ then has probability $1$, so all beliefs are equal
Beliefs at $h$ must then be uniform, so $\sigma$ plays no role
The ratio $\mathbb{P}(x)/\mathbb{P}(h)$ defining $\mathbb{P}(x\mid h)$ divides by $0$
No player moves at $h$, so a belief there is not needed

questions.question: After entry, an incumbent holds belief $\mu=\frac{1}{3}$ that the entrant is competitive (the prior was $0.1$). Fight pays $-4$ against a competitive entrant and $1$ against a weak one; Accommodate pays $0$. What should the incumbent do?
options: Fight, since Fight has expected payoff $0.5$ under the prior $0.1$
Accommodate, since Fight has expected payoff $-\frac{2}{3}<0$
Fight, since the weak entrant is the more likely node
Mix, since any belief strictly between $0$ and $1$ makes both optimal

questions.question: Two assessments $(\sigma,\mu)$ and $(\sigma,\mu')$ have the same $\sigma$; under $\sigma$, information set $h$ is reached with probability $0$, and $\mu$ and $\mu'$ differ only at $h$. Which statement is correct?
options: Bayes' rule fixes the belief at $h$ uniquely, so at most one local distribution is admissible.
Both beliefs are admissible at $h$ under Bayes' rule, and the optimal action there may differ.
The beliefs at $h$ are irrelevant, as $h$ is never reached under $\sigma$
They must coincide at $h$, since both must equal the prior probabilities

questions.question: In a finite extensive-form game with perfect recall, for a node $x$ in an information set $h$ that is reached with positive probability, why does the belief consistent with $\sigma$ equal $\mathbb{P}_\sigma(x)/\mathbb{P}_\sigma(h)$?
options: The nodes of $h$ are independent events, so their probabilities can be divided
Reaching $x$ implies reaching $h$, so $\mathbb{P}_\sigma(\{x\}\cap h)=\mathbb{P}_\sigma(x)$
The event $h$ has probability $1$ whenever a player moves at it
Each node of $h$ is equally likely, so the ratio counts the nodes of $h$

questions.question: Nature picks type $t_1$ or $t_2$ for player 1, each with probability $\frac{1}{2}$. Type $t_1$ plays $U$ with probability $0.8$, type $t_2$ with probability $0.2$; otherwise $D$. Player 2 sees only $U$ or $D$. What are $\big(\mu(t_1\mid U),\ \mu(t_1\mid D)\big)$?

Player 1 chooses $L$, $M$ or $R$; $R$ ends the game, and after $L$ or $M$ player 2 moves at one information set $\{x_L,x_M\}$. For which mixed strategy $(L,M,R)$ of player 1 is $\mu(x_L)=\frac{3}{4}$ the only belief that agrees with it?
